full_judgment:
24. In the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 56, it is stated that even if there is previous sanction such transfer shall not be validated if it is in contravention of any other law, that is, if any other law prohibits such transfer, any lease exceeding five years even with the previous sanction of the Administrator shall be invalid. Now it is to be looked into whether the lease in question has been granted in violation of any existing law, that is, the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 (Act, 1949) and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act, 1950). The answer to this point depends upon the determination of the nature of the land transferred and the application of those laws in the context of the execution of the deed in question. Admittedly, the suit land is situated within Sylhet City Corporation area and the nature of the suit land has been mentioned as (Bangla) (vegetable garden). Thus the suit land is non-agricultural land. 'Non-agricultural land' within section 2(4) of the Act, 1949 means "land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for the purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purpose...... 

 25. A land which was originally leased for agricultural or horticultural purposes but is being used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture without the consent of the landlord and if the period for which the land has been so used is less than twelve years will not be included in the category of 'non-agricultural land' in view of section 2(4)(b). This exception is not applicable to this case in view of the admitted fact that the lease was granted not for a period less than twelve years. So the primary test in determining a particular land is non-agricultural or not, rests firstly as to whether the land is a 'non-agricultural land' as defined in the Act of 1949, and secondly, the purpose for which the tenancy was created. 

 28. The defendant's tenancy was created after the Act of 1949 came into force in 1965, and therefore, he was an under-tenant within the meaning of Act, 1949 during the relevant times. Section 4 provided the purpose for which a non-agricultural tenant may hold non-agricultural land i.e. for (a) homestead or residential purposes; (b) manufacturing or business purposes; or (c) religious or other purposes. The word 'homestead' includes gardens, tanks and land necessary for enjoyment as home-stead. Under section 2(14) of the Act, 1950, the word 'homestead' means a dwelling house with the land under it, together with any court-yard, garden, tank, place of worship and private burial or cremation ground attached and appertaining to such dwelling house, and includes any out-buildings used for the purpose of enjoying the dwelling house or for purposes connected with agricultural or horticulture and such lands within well-defined limits, whether vacant or not, as are treated to be appertaining thereto. 

 31. Since there is no allegation of violation of section 6 no discussion on this provision is called for. Section 7 provides the rights and liabilities of the tenants in respect of a tenancy created before or after the commencement of the Transfer of Property Act, and in case of a lease created in writing for a period not less than twelve years, and if the landlord has allowed the tenant to raise constructions or structures before the expiry period of lease, then the ten-ant holding the non-agricultural land shall not be ejected by the landlord on any grounds other than for the purposes specified in the section. In case of death of the tenant his heirs shall inherit the tenanted property. These protections provided to an under-tenant in Chapter IV would be applicable to the defendant if section 26A had not been inserted in the Act of 1949 in 1967 but the scenario has totally been changed after the amendment. 

 32. Section 23 of the Act provides the manner of transfer of non-agricultural land. It is provided that every transfer of the non-agricultural land by a non-agricultural tenant shall be made by registered instrument. The lease in question was executed by a registered instrument and thus, the lease satisfied the requirements of section 23. There is another aspect which is very much important for resolving the dispute in controversy. After the acquisition of rent receiving interest, there was restriction for sub-letting of any land by section 75A of the Act, 1950 which was inserted by Act XII of 1954. Under this provision the creation of a subordinate tenancy was prohibited and/or invalidated. Under the amendment the rent-receivers were themselves to retain certain classes of retainable khas land as tenant directly under the Government. They were restricted to create further sub-tenancies under them. The creation of sub-tenancy was validated which were effected before the publication of the Notification under sections 17(3) or 31(1) of the said Act. Similar prohibition for sub-letting has been provided in section 26A (1) of Act, 1949 by the East Pakistan Ordinance No. IX of 1967, which provides, Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non-agricultural tenant shall sub-let the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms or conditions whatsoever. 

 35. Next the question to be considered is whether in view of section 70 of Act, 1949, the defendant can be evicted by the plaintiff in execution of a decree of civil Court. Section 70 pro-vides non-agricultural tenant shall be ejected from the tenancy or from any non-agricultural land which he holds except in execution of a decree of a competent civil Court". This provision clearly suggests that a non-agricultural tenant can be evicted by the landlord through a decree of a civil Court. This section is in part materia with section 89 of Bengal Tenancy Act. The effect of this section is to limit the landlord the right of ejectment under the Act. This section was in existence in the original Act of 1949 with a view to protect the tenants from being evicted by the landlords from non-agricultural land other than by due process of law. This section becomes obsolete after section 26A has come into force. 

 36. Section 83 of Act, 1950 provides that a raiyat shall have the right to occupy and use the land comprised in his holding in any manner he likes. With the acquisition of lands of different classes of rent receivers, rent receiving interest extends up to the end of Part IV. The second division starts with Part V and extends upto the end of Act, 1950. Different provisions of Part V became operative in different areas or districts from the date of publication of notifications and thereupon Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed on those areas or districts. All holders of land within the areas in respect of which compensation assessment-roll has been published, became tenants under the Government. Section 81A of Act, 1950 provides rights and liabilities of non-agricultural tenants. It says; 

 "(1) Except as otherwise provided in this Part, the rights and liabilities a holder of non-agricultural land, who has become a tenant under the Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such-land under the pro-visions of this Act, shall, where the provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, applied to such land, at the time of such acquisition, be regulated by provisions of that Act. 

 39. If a non-agricultural tenant sub-lets his tenancy or a part thereof in contravention of subsection (1), the tenancy shall be extinguished and shall vest in the Government as per sub-section (2) of section 26A. When the lease under consideration was created this pro-vision was nonexistent. As observed above, the defendant was an under-tenant when the tenancy was created. Now the question for consideration is to determine the status of the defendant after insertion of section 26A. On a combined reading of sections 81 and 82(8), there is no gainsaying that a sub-tenant or under-tenant created by a tenant has matured his status as a tenant/malik under the Act of 1949 on and from the date of section 26A coming into force. 40. In Province of East Pakistan vs Muhammad Hossain, 16 DLR (SC) 667, the question arose for consideration was whether after the acquisition of rent receiving interest, a tenancy created by a rent-receiver in respect Of non-agricultural land is hit by section 75A or in the alternative there is conflict between section 9 and 75A of the Act. It was observed by H. Rahman, J. 'Section 75A, though it came into force on the 30th August 1954, was made operative only from the date or notification under section 11 (3) or section 31 (1) and, as such, it had no retrospective operation and did not invalidate leases created before such date." Similar principle will be applicable to the case of defendant whose lease was created prior to the insertion of section 26A. 

 42. The purpose of omitting the word 'sub-lease' by Ordinance IX of 1967 as evident is only for the purpose of avoiding preemption under section 24 of the Act. In the said Act the word 'sub-let' has not been defined. Only the word 'under-tenant' has been defined in section 3(3). The use of the expression 'sublet' in my view is misnomer, inasmuch as, if we read this provision along with sections 3, 21 and 22, the intention of the Legislature will be discernible. The expression 'sub-lease' or 'sublet' have been used in the same context of the term 'under-tenant' and they are used in cognate sense. A sub-ordinate tenancy under which an under-tenant would be liable to pay for that land to a person other than the Government is liable pay to the Government after section 26A came into force and his status has been upgraded to a tenant/malik. In other words, after insertion of section 26A by Ordinance No.IX of 1967, there is one category of non-agricultural tenant on and from 22nd December, 1967 and the defendant is a tenant/malik under the Government and whatever right the plaintiff had in respect of the suit land extinguished from that date. Thus, there is no violation of section 26A or any other provisions of the Act, 1949 or Act, 1950. Now the rights which have been given to a raiyat under section 83 of the Act, 1950 can also be exercised by a under-tenant created before 1967, such as, to occupy and use the non-agricultural land in any manner he likes. 

 49. The Court of Appeal below committed another fundamental error in assuming that no lease of immovable property could be granted other than a lease for occupation of the land for a limited period. Further, the Court of Appeal below compared creation of the tenancy with the settlement of land made by ex-landlords under the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1985 on a misconception of law. The Court of Appeal below ought to have ascertained the nature of the land, the laws applicable to such lease and the construction of the deed before deciding the question on whether the mutawalli of a waqf estate has power, to transfer a portion of the waqf property by way of lease for a period exceeding 5 years. As observed above, the lease was created in respect of non-agricultural land. A tenant holding non-agricultural land under a lease in writing for a period exceeding twelve years shall not be ejected by the landlord on any grounds other than the grounds specified in section 4 of Act 1949 and his interest shall, in case of death, be devolved upon his heirs in view of clauses (i) and (ii) respectively of sub-section (3) of section 7. Similarly in case of a tenancy created to an 'under-tenant' corresponding rights of protection have been given be sections 20, 21 and 22 of the Act, 1949. 

 51. In the case of leases for agricultural or manufacturing purposes, the presumption will be that they are from year to year and in the case of other leases the tenancy is deemed to be from month to month. In the former case a six month's notice is necessary for terminating lease and in the latter case fifteen days notice is necessary. These provisions are quite distinguishable and not applicable to the case of the defendant in view of the discussions made above. The Court of Appeal below approached the matter on wrong premise in considering the lease in question and such wrong approach had reflected in the latter part of the judgment. It has not explained why a lease of non-agricultural land granted with prior sanction of the Administrator in respect of any part of Waqf property by the mutawalli for the welfare of the waqf estate would be illegal. The High Court Division on consideration of section 56 of the Ordinance has rightly approved the views of the trial Court. The High Court Division held that the lease having been created with prior sanction of the Administrator was legal and valid. Accordingly, the High Court Division has rightly found that the plaintiff's suit is not maintainable and is liable to be dismissed.
